mechaber.he:
תולדות הבור כגון אבנו סכינו ומשאו שהזיקו. ובו ז סעיפים:
תולדות הבור אבנו סכינו ומשאו וכיוצא בהן שהניח' בר"ה והזיקו במקומם בין הפקירן או לא הפקירן או שהניחם בראש גגו ונפלו ברוח מצוי' והזיקו במקומם אחר שנחו שדומה לבור ממונו שמזיק במקום שמונח שם לפיכך יש לו כל דיני בור לחייב נזק שלם מתחלתו על מיתת בהמ' או הזיק' ועל נזקי אדם בין נתקל באבן והוזק באבן בין נתקל בקרקע והוזק באבן אבל אם נתקל באבן והוזק בקרקע פטור (ופטור) בו ממיתת אדם ונזקי כלים וכן אם הניחם ברשותו והפקיר רשותו ולא הפקירם ונתקל בקרקע וניזק בתקל' זו והוזק חייב בעל התקלה:
mechaber.en:
Derivatives of a pit, such as one's stone, knife, or burden that caused damage. It contains seven seifim:
The derivatives of a pit include one's stone, knife, burden, and similar objects that one left in the public domain and that caused damage where they lay, whether he abandoned ownership of them or not. The same applies if he placed them on top of his roof, they fell in an ordinary wind, and after coming to rest they caused damage where they lay, for this resembles a pit: his property causes damage in the place where it rests. They therefore have all the laws of a pit, including liability for full damages from the outset for the death or injury of an animal and for injury to a person, whether the victim tripped over the stone and was injured by the stone or tripped on the ground and was injured by the stone. But if he tripped over the stone and was injured by the ground, the owner of the obstacle is exempt and is exempt from liability for the death of a person and for damage to utensils. Likewise, if he left these objects on his own property, then abandoned his property but not the objects, and someone tripped on the ground and was injured by this obstacle, the owner of the obstacle is liable.

With utensils. But if the owner of the courtyard himself was injured by them, the owner of the animal is liable. Although the verse states 'when a man digs a pit,' excluding a pit created by an ox, here the material belonged to the animal's owner at the time it fell, and he had the duty to remove it, so it is as though he dug the pit himself. Although siman 313 explains that if Reuven's animal deposited dung in Shimon's courtyard, Shimon acquires the dung, here the owner of the courtyard does not wish his property to acquire an object that can injure him. If it is evident that the owner of the courtyard already knew of the dung, was pleased with it, and his courtyard acquired it for him, and he was later injured by it, the owner of the animal is exempt. A pit is exempt for utensils. But if the courtyard owner himself is injured by the excrement, the animal owner can be liable because the excrement is his pit. Although Scripture says, "if a man digs a pit," excluding an ox that digs a pit, here the animal owner owned the excrement at the time it was deposited, and the duty to remove the danger rested upon him. It is therefore treated as though he himself dug it. Although siman 313 states that if Reuven's animal deposits dung in Shimon's courtyard, Shimon's courtyard acquires the dung, this case differs because the courtyard owner does not want his courtyard to acquire something dangerous that may injure him. If it is clear that he already knew of the dung and was pleased to have it, then his courtyard acquires it. If he is later injured by it, the animal owner is exempt.
